answerNotes.CROSSWALK: A crosswalk is a marked place to cross a road. The signal gives instructions; the striped crossing itself does not control traffic.
answerNotes.SIGNAL: A signal communicates an instruction. At a crossing it can use lights or symbols rather than spoken words.
answerNotes.CURB: A curb is the raised edge between roadway and sidewalk. The corner is where streets meet, not another name for that raised edge.
answerNotes.STREET: A street is a road through a built-up area. Its name and building numbers form part of a postal address.
answerNotes.LIGHT: Light makes things visible. A lamp produces light, while a mirror mainly reflects light arriving from elsewhere.
answerNotes.CORNER: A corner is where two edges meet. In a jigsaw, a corner piece normally has two outer edges.
answerNotes.STOP: Stop asks for movement to end. At a crossing, it concerns waiting for the appropriate signal rather than a kind of destination.
answerNotes.BUTTON: A button fastens through a buttonhole or loop. Some have holes through the face; others attach by a small shank on the back.

answerNotes.METER: A parking meter records paid parking time. Meter can also name other measuring devices, so the street scene supplies the intended meaning.
answerNotes.COIN: A coin is a metal piece of money. The value depends on the currency and period; Bible stories do not use modern U.S. coins.
answerNotes.CURB: A curb is the raised edge between roadway and sidewalk. The corner is where streets meet, not another name for that raised edge.
answerNotes.CAR: A car carries people on roads. Its trunk holds luggage, while the passenger compartment holds the seats.
answerNotes.STREET: A street is a road through a built-up area. Its name and building numbers form part of a postal address.
answerNotes.SIGN: Sign can be a public notice or the action of writing a name. Check whether the clue describes an object or asks for a verb.
answerNotes.HOUR: An hour contains sixty minutes. A minute contains sixty seconds; these two relationships are easy to mix up.
answerNotes.WHEEL: A wheel rotates around an axle. Its tire is an outer covering, not another name for the entire wheel.
answerNotes.STOP: Stop asks for movement to end. At a crossing, it concerns waiting for the appropriate signal rather than a kind of destination.
answerNotes.TICKET: A ticket can give admission or identify an item left for a service. A theater ticket and a dry-cleaning claim ticket serve different uses.

Family vehicle with seats and a trunk

United States liquid unit used in gasoline sales

answerNotes.GAS: Gas is the usual American short name for gasoline. The pump sells a liquid fuel despite the short word's other meaning.
answerNotes.PUMP: A pump moves liquid. A faucet or tap controls the opening through which the liquid comes out.
answerNotes.HOSE: A hose is a flexible tube. A nozzle shapes the flow at one end, while a tap controls its supply at the other.
answerNotes.CAR: A car carries people on roads. Its trunk holds luggage, while the passenger compartment holds the seats.
answerNotes.FUEL: Fuel provides energy when an engine or heater uses it. Gasoline is one fuel; the general word does not mean gasoline alone.
answerNotes.PRICE: Price is the amount asked for an item. Change is money returned after a customer pays more than that amount.
answerNotes.RECEIPT: A receipt records a completed payment. A bill asks for payment, so the two papers serve different purposes.
answerNotes.HANDLE: A handle is the part made for the hand to grip. Its shape depends on whether the object is carried, pulled, poured, or turned.

answerNotes.DASHBOARD: A dashboard places instruments and controls in front of the driver. Gauges display information rather than doing the steering.
answerNotes.KEY: A door key is shaped to match a particular lock. A spare is another key kept for use if the main one is unavailable.
answerNotes.WHEEL: A wheel rotates around an axle. Its tire is an outer covering, not another name for the entire wheel.
answerNotes.MIRROR: A mirror reflects light to form an image. Cleaning the surface removes marks; it does not change the reflected object.
answerNotes.FUEL: Fuel provides energy when an engine or heater uses it. Gasoline is one fuel; the general word does not mean gasoline alone.
answerNotes.LIGHT: Light makes things visible. A lamp produces light, while a mirror mainly reflects light arriving from elsewhere.
answerNotes.RADIO: A radio receives broadcasts. Choosing a station selects a particular transmission rather than changing the recorded song itself.
answerNotes.CLOCK: A clock shows time. The hour hand moves more slowly than the minute hand on a traditional clock face.

answerNotes.SCHOOL: School memories vary between generations. These scenes select familiar older objects without assuming every reader used the same equipment.
answerNotes.SIGN: Sign can be a public notice or the action of writing a name. Check whether the clue describes an object or asks for a verb.
answerNotes.STOP: Stop asks for movement to end. At a crossing, it concerns waiting for the appropriate signal rather than a kind of destination.
answerNotes.STREET: A street is a road through a built-up area. Its name and building numbers form part of a postal address.
answerNotes.HAND: Hand can name a body part or a clock pointer. A clock's minute hand makes a full turn each hour.
answerNotes.CORNER: A corner is where two edges meet. In a jigsaw, a corner piece normally has two outer edges.
answerNotes.CURB: A curb is the raised edge between roadway and sidewalk. The corner is where streets meet, not another name for that raised edge.
answerNotes.FLAG: A flag can be a cloth symbol or a small signaling marker. A mailbox flag shows a postal signal rather than identifying a country.
